source: Consistent with previous studies (Harapan et al., 2020; Detoc et al., 2020), HCW were more accepting the vaccine, although with still low proportions of about one in four (18% yes and 7.1% depending on the type).
evidence: This is supported by the study's data and comparison with previous research.

claim: A study on Congolese HCW conducted in March–April, 2020 reported a similar notably low rate of acceptance (only 27.7%).
source: One study on Congolese HCW (n = 613) conducted in March–April, 2020 reported a similar notably low rate of acceptance (only 27.7%) (Kabamba Nzaji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Participants between the ages of 30 and 59 were less willing to receive vaccination compared with older participants.
source: Participants between the ages of 30 and 59 were less willing to receive vaccination compared with older participants, an expected result given the fact that COVID-19 severity is associated with older age.
evidence: This is supported by the study's data with interpretation based on known COVID-19 risk factors.

claim: Younger participants (<29 years old) showed more willingness to be vaccinated.
source: However, younger participants (<29 years old) showed more willingness to be vaccinated.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: Among the 29 different reasons for vaccine rejection/hesitancy, the top two reasons selected by the respondents reflected concerns about safety, while the next three most prevalent reasons were issues of distrust.
source: Among the 29 different reasons for vaccine rejection/hesitancy, the top two reasons selected by the respondents reflected concerns about safety, while the next three most prevalent reasons were issues of distrust.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on barriers to vaccination.

claim: High levels of distrust and concern about safety are consistent with the literature.
source: This is consistent with the literature, which showed high levels of distrust and concern about safety (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's findings with previous research.

claim: The three forms of distrust (in health care policies, in vaccine expedited production and in published studies) were notably higher among respondents residing in the Arab countries than those living outside the Arab world.
source: The three forms of distrust (in health care policies, in vaccine expedited production and in published studies) were notably higher among respondents residing in the Arab countries than those living outside the Arab world.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's comparative findings.

claim: More residents of the Arab world believe that the vaccine has not been tested on a large enough number of people.
source: The same applies to the belief that the vaccine has not been tested on a large enough number of people, just tens or hundreds, which reflects less awareness of the vaccine development process in the Arab countries and highlights the need to educate the general public on the subject.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings with interpretation.

claim: More residents of the Arab world believe that the vaccine is not necessary anymore because most people in the participant's country 'have already been infected' or because the infection rate is decreasing.
source: Similarly, more residents of the Arab world believe that the vaccine is not necessary anymore because most people in the participant's country 'have already been infected' or because the infection rate is decreasing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: Promoting voluntary acceptance is a better route and coercion should be avoided.
source: Lazarus et al.'s large-scale study indicated that promoting voluntary acceptance is a better route and that coercion should be avoided (Lazarus et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A systematic review indicated that 'mandates could increase resistance'.
source: Similarly, a systematic review indicated that 'mandates could increase resistance' (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a systematic review.

claim: The majority of participants (59.5%) believed that vaccination should be left to individual choices.
source: In our study, the majority of participants (59.5%) believed that vaccination should be left to individual choices and only a minority believed it should be mandated for certain categories of people (6.1%) or on populations in which the vaccine was proven to be effective and safe as per clinical studies (13.6%).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: Approximately one-fifth of respondents chose 'The vaccine might lose its efficacy against the new viral strains' as a reason for hesitation.
source: Approximately one-fifth of our respondents chose 'The vaccine might lose its efficacy against the new viral strains' as a reason for hesitation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: The survey was published shortly after reports of the new viral strains in the UK and South Africa have been made public.
source: The survey was published shortly after reports of the new viral strains in the UK and South Africa have been made public, and with the recent reports of decreased efficacy of some vaccines (Kabamba Nzaji et al., 2020; The Guardian, 2021; Knoll and Wonodi, 2021), this concern of efficacy is expected to increase among the public.
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of the survey with citations to news about vaccine efficacy.

claim: The response to the question of willingness is broken down from Yes/No or Likert scale to a spectrum of choices which could more accurately detect the hesitant respondents.
source: First of all, the response to the question of willingness is broken down from Yes/No or Likert scale (in previous works) to a spectrum of choices which could more accurately detect the hesitant respondents who could have otherwise chosen (Yes) or (Agree/Strongly agree).
evidence: This is an explanation of the study's methodological approach.

claim: In a large-scale survey conducted in October 2020 that included 18,526 adults across 15 countries, 73% strongly agreed or agreed that 'if a vaccine for COVID-19 were available, I would get it'.
source: In a large-scale survey conducted in October 2020 that included 18,526 adults across 15 countries (Ipsos, 2020), 73% strongly agreed or agreed that 'if a vaccine for COVID-19 were available, I would get it'.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous survey.

claim: Of those who agreed to get vaccinated in the Ipsos survey, only 22% agreed that they would become vaccinated 'immediately after the vaccine is available'.
source: However, of those, only 22% agreed that they would become vaccinated 'immediately after the vaccine is available', while some others chose that they would wait for a year and even longer.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous survey.

claim: The WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization defined vaccine hesitancy as a 'delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite the availability of vaccination services' in 2015.
source: In 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO) Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization defined vaccine hesitancy as a 'delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccination despite the availability of vaccination services' (MacDonald, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the WHO definition.

claim: 20.8% of the participants chose 'I will wait and see its effects on others'.
source: In the present study, 20.8% of the participants chose (I will wait and see its effects on others) – many of whom could have possibly chosen (Yes) or (Agree) had the waiting choice been eliminated.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings with interpretation.

claim: A systematic review noted that 'When answer options included different timings for vaccination, more people chose to wait than get it as soon as possible'.
source: A systematic review noted that 'When answer options included different timings for vaccination, more people chose to wait than get it as soon as possible' and that the two answer choices (Yes/No) received relatively high affirmatives (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a systematic review.

claim: Only 3 of about 70 studies and polls in the systematic review included the choice of 'wait a while until others have taken it' for the question of vaccine acceptance.
source: Only 3 of about 70 studies and polls in this review included the choice of 'wait a while until others have taken it' for the question of vaccine acceptance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a systematic review.

claim: In the three polls that included the waiting option, the percentage of those who chose that they would take the vaccine as soon as they can was low (21–28%).
source: In these three polls, conducted before vaccine availability, the percentage of those who chose that they would take the vaccine as soon as they can (or as soon as possible) was low (21–28%).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous polls.

claim: Vaccine acceptance may be overestimated in many studies.
source: This indicates that vaccine acceptance may be overestimated in many studies and highlights the need to redefine vaccine acceptance in a uniform way among different studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of previous studies.

claim: Social and political differences were found to have a prominent effect on COVID-19 vaccine acceptance.
source: Social and political differences were found to have a prominent effect on COVID-19 vaccine acceptance, especially that many people assumed political interference in the vaccine and in the pandemic itself (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a systematic review.

claim: Vaccine acceptance was lower in Arab countries in previous studies: Jordan (37.4%), Saudi (64.72%) and (44.7%), and in a small multinational survey that included several countries, mainly Jordan and Kuwait (29.4%).
source: Vaccine acceptance was lower in Arab countries in previous studies: Jordan (37.4%) (El-Elimat et al., 2020), Saudi (64.72%) (Al-Mohaithef and Padhi, 2020) and (44.7%) (Magadmi and Kamel, 2020), and in a small multinational survey that included several countries, mainly Jordan and Kuwait (29.4%) (Sallam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The chronological analysis of vaccine acceptance and time does not show a linear relationship.
source: The chronological analysis of vaccine acceptance and time – in local and multinational studies – does not show a linear relationship – if anything, the public's acceptance can be best described as fluctuating.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of previous studies over time.

claim: Several surveys conducted in the last third of 2020 have shown a decrease in vaccination acceptance compared with previous surveys.
source: Several surveys conducted in the last third of 2020 have shown a decrease in vaccination acceptance compared with previous surveys (Lin et al., 2020; Ipsos, 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Kreps et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous surveys.

claim: The intent to vaccinate has declined in 10 of the 15 countries from August to October 2020.
source: For example, the intent to vaccinate has declined in 10 of the 15 countries from August to October 2020 (Ipsos, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous survey.

claim: A systematic review of publications until 20 October 2020 showed declining vaccine acceptance (from >70% in March to <50% in October) with demographic, socioeconomic, and partisan divides observed.
source: A systematic review of publications until 20 October 2020 showed declining vaccine acceptance (from >70% in March to <50% in October) with demographic, socioeconomic, and partisan divides observed (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a systematic review.

claim: A more recent multinational survey conducted from November 2020 to mid-January 2021 in 15 countries and a study conducted from 28 to 31 January 2020 in 14 countries have both shown an increase in vaccine acceptance.
source: However, a more recent multinational survey conducted from November 2020 to mid-January 2021 in 15 countries (Imperial College London, 2021) and a study conducted from 28 to 31 January 2020 in 14 countries Ipsos, 2021 have both shown an increase in vaccine acceptance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent surveys.

claim: The more recent studies in Arab countries show lower acceptance rates than the earlier ones.
source: As for Arab countries, the more recent studies (Sallam et al., 2021; El-Elimat et al., 2020; Hussein, 2021) show lower acceptance rates than the earlier ones.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in Arab countries.

claim: A study conducted in Egypt during March 2020 found out that about 73.0% were looking forward to getting the vaccine when available.
source: For example, A study conducted in Egypt (n = 559) during March 2020 found out that about 73.0% were looking forward to getting the vaccine when available (Al-Mohaithef and Padhi, 2020; Magadmi and Kamel, 2020; Abdelhafiz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to a previous study.

claim: A more recent study on HCW in Egypt during December 2020 concluded that only 13.5% totally agree to receiving the vaccine and 32.4% somewhat agree.
source: However, the more recent study on HCW in Egypt (n = 496) during December 2020 concluded that only 13.5% totally agree to receiving the vaccine and 32.4% somewhat agree (Hussein, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the current survey, 17.0% and 24.0% of participants in Egypt (general and HCW, respectively) were willing to take the vaccine.
source: In our survey that is more recent than the mentioned studies, 17.0% and 24.0% of participants in Egypt (general [n = 5339] and HCW [n = 1250], respectively) were willing to take the vaccine.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: A Saudi Arabia study published in May 2020 observed that 64.7% of participants showed interest to accept the COVID-19 vaccine if it is available.
source: A Saudi Arabia study published in May 2020 observed that 64.7% of participants (n = 1000) showed interest to accept the COVID-19 vaccine if it is available (Al-Mohaithef and Padhi, 2020), and another study conducted during May (n = 3101) showed a 44.7% acceptance rate (Magadmi and Kamel, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In a more recent study in Saudi Arabia published in December 2020, 31.8% of participants showed acceptance.
source: However, in a more recent study in Saudi Arabia too, published in December 2020, 31.8% of participants (n = 154) showed acceptance (Sallam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the current survey, 19.8% of participants from Saudi Arabia showed acceptance.
source: In our survey that is more recent than the mentioned studies, 19.8% of participants from Saudi Arabia (n = 3588) showed acceptance.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: Health care workers (HCWs) are at increased risk of acquiring and transmitting COVID-19 infection.
source: Health care workers (HCWs) are at increased risk of acquiring and transmitting COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about COVID-19 transmission.

claim: HCWs present role models for communities with regards to attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination.
source: Moreover, they present role models for communities with regards to attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination.
evidence: This is a statement based on the social role of healthcare workers.

claim: Vaccine hesitancy in HCWs is of a special concern.
source: Therefore, vaccine hesitancy in this group is of a special concern, and we discussed hesitancy in Arab healthcare workers elsewhere (Qunaibi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of HCWs with citation to another publication.

claim: Being an online survey, the study may have under-represented certain groups of individuals, including members of older age groups and those who are not active on social media.
source: Being an online survey, our study may have under-represented certain groups of individuals, including members of older age groups and those who are not active on social media.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation of the study methodology.

claim: The study cannot rule out selection bias that might have affected the results.
source: We cannot rule out selection bias that might have affected our results.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation of the study.

claim: The large number of participants and the consistency of results in different countries that were geographically close and similar socioeconomically confirm the reliability of the survey.
source: We believe that the large number of participants and the consistency of results in different countries that were geographically close and similar socioeconomically confirm the reliability of our survey.
evidence: This is an inference about the study's reliability based on its characteristics.

claim: The high vaccine hesitancy could further compromise the economies of Arab countries in addition to the pandemic health hazard.
source: Given that the vaccine is being purchased from state expenditure, the high vaccine hesitancy could further compromise the economies of Arab countries in addition to the pandemic health hazard.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the economic implications of vaccine hesitancy.

claim: Mandating the vaccine is not a desirable choice and could further increase the distrust.
source: At the same time, mandating the vaccine is not a desirable choice and could further increase the distrust.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings about distrust and previous literature.

claim: The study needs to be replicated at a later time to measure the change in public acceptance.
source: With the highly dynamic nature of the pandemic and vaccine production process and the interplay of ever-changing factors that affect vaccine acceptance, our study needs to be replicated at a later time to measure the change in public acceptance.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the dynamic nature of the pandemic.

claim: There is a need to create a uniform definition for vaccine acceptance in the surveys to avoid misestimation.
source: The high proportion of people willing to wait until others have received the vaccine and the unavailability of the preferred vaccine for others show a need to create a uniform definition for vaccine acceptance in the surveys to avoid misestimation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings and analysis of previous research.
